profile.campus: Sunnyvale, California (Equinix SV6, Silicon Valley network)
profile.reading:
This is Equinix's SV6 facility at 444 Toyama Drive in Sunnyvale, California, part of the company's dense Silicon Valley interconnection network anchored by facilities across San Jose, Santa Clara, Palo Alto, and Sunnyvale. Equinix was founded in Silicon Valley in 1998 by former Digital Equipment Corporation facilities managers Al Avery and Jay Adelson on the premise of providing a neutral place for competing networks to interconnect, and remains headquartered nearby in Redwood City; the company converted to a real estate investment trust in January 2015 and trades on Nasdaq as EQIX. Equinix markets its Silicon Valley buildings, SV6 included, as serving what it calls the largest concentration of high-tech companies and peering hubs in the world, with access to major financial and enterprise networks, typically backed by N+1 power and cooling redundancy, a 99.9999%-plus global guaranteed uptime commitment, and certifications including ISO 27001, HIPAA, and SOC 2 Type II across the company's standardized Silicon Valley building specifications. This session's fetch of Equinix's SV6 page (via the equinix.co.uk mirror recorded in OSM) did not return SV6's own individual square footage or power capacity figures, so this registry records the general Silicon Valley campus specification pattern, drawn from SV1, SV4, and SV8's individually confirmed figures, as regional context rather than a confirmed fact for this specific building.

Silicon Valley Power, Sunnyvale's municipal utility, has cited sustained data center load growth across the San Jose-Santa Clara-Sunnyvale corridor in its own capacity planning, a dynamic distinct from newer data center markets given how built-out and power-constrained the Bay Area grid already is after decades of continuous data center development since Equinix's own 1998 founding in the area.

reading.body:
Equinix SV6 is one of twelve facilities in Silicon Valley under Equinix's control, serving over 10,500 customers across enterprises and network providers, though the operator publishes no power consumption or capacity figures for individual buildings.

Equinix's opacity about per-facility power draw is typical among the largest colocation operators. The company discloses regional footprints and customer counts but withholds the specific megawatts consumed at each site, forcing researchers to infer capacity from real estate footprint or industry estimates rather than direct measurement. This matters because data center power consumption is the most direct proxy for AI training and inference infrastructure, yet remains largely proprietary.

SV6 sits in Sunnyvale, part of Equinix's larger Silicon Valley campus that spans multiple cities. The facility's location in the Bay Area situates it within the highest-density AI and cloud computing market in the United States. Whether SV6 runs at full power utilization, and how much of that power goes to AI workloads versus other tenants, remains unknown from published sources.

The gap between what Equinix discloses and what the compute constraint requires is significant. Understanding whether the grid binding constraint is real demands megawatt counts by facility and by customer. Until operators publish this data, estimates of AI scaling's power ceiling rest on aggregated utility filings and inference from acquisition announcements rather than operational fact.
